div.p: 1117 Pollux 2. 154 ἀχείρωτον δὲ Σοφοκλῆς εἴρηκε τὸ ἀχειρούργητον, δυσχείρωτα δὲ Δημοσθένης (61. 37).

Nauck is almost alone in denying that Pollux is quoting from O.C. 698 φύτευμ᾿ ἀχείρωτον αὐτοποιόν, where see Jebb's n. It may be observed that the occurrence of αὐτοποιόν there would be likely to suggest the false interpretation given by Pollux: in most contexts such an inducement would be absent. But it has not been explained why Suid. and Bekk. anecd. p. 474, 4 have the unintelligible gloss ἀχείρωτον· ἄμωμον.

1118 Phot. ed. Reitz. p. 36, 17 (Phryn. praep. soph. p. 37, 23; Bekk. anecd. p. 347, 26) Σοφοκλῆς δὲ τὴν εὐθεῖαν εἶπεν ἀείζως γενεά (fr. 740)· ἀπὸ δὲ τῆς ζωὸς δισυλλάβου εὐθείας φιλόζωος εἶπεν ὁ κωμικὸς Πλάτων (ὁ κ. Πλ. om. Bekk. anecd.).
The new codex of Photius shows that this fragment belongs to Plato the comic poet, and not to Sophocles.

1119 Priscian. inst. Gr. 18. 206 (II p. 308, 20) iustum pro vero et verum pro iusto frequenter tam nos quam Attici ponimus. Sophocles Αἴαντι ῾δίκαιος γόνος.᾿ id. 17. 168 (II p. 193, 18) iuste pro vere ... Euripides Αἴαντι ῾δίκαιος γόνος᾿ pro ἀληθής.

Sophocles thrice uses δικαίως in the sense of ἀληθῶς: O.T. 852 οὔτοι ποτ᾿, ὦναξ, τόν γε Λαΐου φόνον | φανεῖ δικαίως ὀρθόν. ib. 1283 ὁ πρὶν παλαιὸς δ᾿ ὄλβος ἦν πάροιθε μὲν | ὄλβος δικαίως. Ai. 547 εἴπερ δικαίως ἔστ᾿ ἐμὸς τὰ πατρόθεν. But this is in accordance with the usage of other authors: Aesch. Theb. 392 ὀρθῶς ἐνδίκως τ᾿ ἐπώνυμον. Eur. fr. 839 ὅθεν οὐκ ἀδίκως | μήτηρ πάντων νενόμισται. Plat. Crat. 418 E (ζυγὸν) ἐπωνόμασται δυογὸν δικαίως. ib. 409 B. Tim. 85 B. Xen. oecon. 21 and many others. [Some of these exx. are due to H.: see also On editing Aeschylus, p. 141.] The adverb
stands on an entirely different footing to that of the adjective; and it is hardly credible that Sophocles used δίκαιος γόνος in the sense of ‘a genuine son,’ for which no parallel has been adduced. (The quotations in L. and S. will not bear examination: Taylor on Aeschin. p. 441 [3. 197] cites them all, as well as others to which the same remark applies.) It seems probable therefore, as has been generally held, that the grammarian intended to quote Ai. 547, and that his memory played him false. The reference to ‘Euripides’ is significant. See also Hesych. II p. 90 ἔνδικον· ἀληθές, which may be a reference to O.T. 1158.

div.p: 1120 Stob. ecl. 2. 31. 5 p. 200, 16 W. Σοφοκλέους. ῾ἐπεὶ. . . πατρός.᾿

I agree with Nauck in thinking that these lines cannot possibly have been written by Sophocles. Dindorf is of the same opinion, but N. Piccolos (Suppl. à l’Anthol. gr. Paris 1853, p. 332) seems to have been the first to doubt their genuineness. See also on fr. 752. The sententious tone, the tameness of the thought, and the entire absence of distinction from the style, are out of keeping with the existing remains of Sophocles. The general cast of the vocabulary, and particularly the use of παιδεύματα (v. 3) and προῖκα (v. 6) in serious verse, suggests a period later than the fifth century. Now, there were two other tragic poets who bore the name of Sophocles and were sufficiently distinguished to have the numbers of their plays recorded in literary chronicles: (1) Sophocles the younger, a grandson of our poet, who exhibited plays from 398 B.C. onwards; (2) a descendant of the same family, belonging to the early part of the second century, who is said to have written fifteen plays: see Haigh, Tragic Drama, p. 445, Susemihl, Gesch. d. gr. Lit. Alexandr. I p. 283. It is not improbable that some of the extracts attributed to their ancestor were actually composed by one or the other of these writers. For these lines Sophocles the younger seems the more likely author. J. writes: ‘The difficulty of conceiving a context in tragedy for these verses is the chief objection to their genuineness. They seem to be spoken either (1) by a παῖς to other παῖδες, or (2) by a mother, or a παιδαγωγός, to young persons — the father being absent (v. 12). The composition of the verses would not in itself warrant their rejection. The last two vv., indeed, are either corrupt or defective. But, apart from this, there is perhaps only one suspicious point in the language — κέκτηται, instead of κτᾶται, in v. 9. Welcker (p. 270) refers these vv. to the Ἐπίγονοι or Ἐριφύλη. He suggests that in the Cyclic Thebais Amphiaraus was described as giving good advice to his young sons, Alcmaeon and Amphilochus, before his own departure for Thebes, from which he knew he was not to return. Welcker supposes that Alcmaeon is here relating (probably in the prologue) his father's departure, and quoting his words of counsel to his sons. But this hypothesis requires a very bold assumption, — viz. that χωρῶμεν refers to the departure of Amphiaraus, and that several words have dropped out after it. The sense was, Welcker imagines, “Let me depart now to Thebes — but do you go to your studies.” A further difficulty in Welcker's view is the use of the first person plural in v. 10 and in v. 12 (φυλαξώμεσθα . . . δοκῶμεν): though this might be defended as = “our family.” ’ Hartung guesses that the lines were spoken by the coryphaeus in the Κρίσις, which had a chorus of Ephebi (!). Meineke (Stob. flor. IV p. xxxiii) believed them genuine, thinking that they were spoken by a παιδαγωγός to the children of Theseus or Heracles, and that τὸ τοῦ θεοῦ in v. 1 refers to a sacrifice for the return of the absent father.

3 f. The traditional pointing is to
put a full stop after παιδεύματα. The objections to this, as the text stands, are conclusive: (1) παιδεύματα must then be in apposition to διδασκαλεῖα, and would require the forced sense ‘means of teaching,’ for which there is no authority; (2) προσλαμβάνειν, unless attached to βελτίονα, would be without an object, since neither παιδεύματα, with the postulated meaning, nor μουσικήν, which is too narrow, could be supplied. To avoid the latter difficulty Hirschig conjectured προσμανθάνειν, which, if adopted, would almost necessarily involve the acceptance of Nauck's λαμβάνειν. Meineke, punctuating as in the text, read παίδευμα γάρ with δεῖ καί for δὲ δεῖ. But neither this alteration nor Wachsmuth's substitution of γάρ for δέ seems to be necessary: for δέ = γάρ see on fr. 576, 4. The position of δέ is no objection: see Jebb on Ai. 116, Headlam, On editing Aeschylus, p. 114, Eur. Hel. 688 (n.). J. preferred the ordinary punctuation, rendering ‘Let us go to the places where the wise (the poets) teach, — to lessons in the lore of the Muses’; but the crucial difficulty is evaded by the break which he assumes after διδασκαλεῖα. — For παιδεύματα as = ‘subjects of instruction,’ see L. and S. and add [Dem.] 60. 16 οἵδε γὰρ ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἐν πᾶσι τοῖς παιδεύμασιν ἦσαν ἐπιφανεῖς. For προσλαμβάνειν cf. [Dem.] 61. 42 ὅλως μὲν γὰρ ἅπασα φύσις βελτίων γίγνεται παιδείαν προσλαβοῦσα τὴν προσήκουσαν. Isocr. 1. 18 ἐὰν ᾖς φιλομαθής, ἔσει πολυμαθής· ἃ μὲν ἐπίστασαι, ταῦτα διαφύλαττε ταῖς μελέταις, ἃ δὲ μὴ μεμάθηκας, προσλάμβανε ταῖς ἐπιστήμαις.

6 Nauck's δ᾿ οὖν is generally accepted, but J. rightly objects that these particles are quite out of place. The proper sense of δ᾿ οὖν is ‘however,’ or, when less strongly adversative, ‘to resume’; here there is no interruption to the thought, which proceeds in orderly sequence. So far as the text is concerned, there is no difficulty in the ellipse of τις — or πᾶς τις — as subject. J. quotes Aesch. Eum. 297 κλύει δὲ καὶ πρόσωθεν ὢν θεός. In sentences of universal import the omission is more common than is generally recognized, and often leads to an unreasonable suspicion of the text: see n. on fr. 951. — προῖκ᾿ ἐπίσταται, ‘readily understands.’ I don't think that προῖκα is used ironically here, but rather that it is shedding its primary application: cf. Antiph. fr. 210 (II 103 K.) ἀρετὴ τὸ προῖκα τοῖς φίλοις ὑπηρετεῖν. For the sentiment cf. Democr. fr. 182 Diels τὰ μὲν καλὰ χρήματα τοῖς πόνοις ἡ μάθησις ἐξεργάζεται, τὰ δ᾿ αἰσχρὰ ἄνευ πόνων αὐτόματα καρποῦται.

8 f. Cf. Eur. Hipp. 380 τὰ χρήστ᾿ ἐπιστάμεσθα καὶ γιγνώσκομεν οὐκ ἐκπονοῦμεν δ᾿, Plat. Prot. 352 D πολλούς φασι γιγνώσκοντας τὰ βέλτιστα οὐκ ἐθέλειν πράττειν, Men. 77 C. — ἀλλὰ κέκτηται: see cr. n. ‘If the vulg. is right, “possesses them with difficulty,” means, “possesses them only after a painful discipline.” ’ (J.) He compares Plat. Theaet. 153 B κτᾶται μαθήματα.

11 f. ὡς ἂν μήτ᾿ . . . κἀποδημοῦντος πατρός. ‘(1) In Eur. I. T. 591 we read, σὺ δ᾿, εἰ γάρ, ὡς ἔοικας, οὔτε δυσγενής, | καὶ τὰς Μυκήνας οἶσθα. This
is very rare [Kuehner-Gerth II 292 quote no other example; but see Wecklein in loc.], though οὔτε . . . τε is not so. And it does not help us here. For here, if we take μήτε . . . καὶ as corresponding, the only tenable version is “that we may not seem to be of the uneducated sort, and that we may seem to be the children of an absent father.” (It is impossible to render, “that we may not seem to be both uneducated, and the children of such a father”: the τε cannot be detached from μήτε, and placed after ἀπαιδεύτων.) Hence we must conclude that the passage suffers from one of two defects. (1) It may be incomplete: i.e. another subjunctive verb may have followed in another verse, the sense being, “that we may not seem uneducated, and also that in our father's absence <we may not neglect our duty>.” Or (2) the text may be corrupt, in which case I would suggest μήτ᾿ ἀκηδοῦντος πατρός.’ (J.) The conjectures mentioned above, with the exception of Herwerden's, do not avoid the difficulty of μήτε . . . καὶ. I have adopted the view that the quotation is incomplete: the contrast to be looked for is between the origin of the persons concerned and their own actions, e.g. μήτ᾿ αὖ σοφῶν γεγῶτες ἀργίᾳ νοσεῖν. H. explained ἀποδημοῦντος πατρός with reference to the phrase ἐκ μέσης τῆς Ἑλλάδος used of the purest Greek origin, as contrasted with the Greek-speaking races of the Levant. He quoted the following illustrations: Liban. epist. 1350 ἐγὼ δέ σε ἠξίουν, ἐκ μέσης ἥκοντα τῆς Ἑλλάδος, γράφειν τι διαφεῦγον τὸν ὄχλον· σὺ δ᾿ ἔοικας ἀμελεῖν λόγων. Liban. IV 363 μὴ τοίνυν νομίζετε τὰ μὲν ἀργυρώνητα ταῦτα ἀνδράποδα, ὄντα τὰ πολλὰ ἐκ Καρίας καὶ Φρυγίας οὕτως εἶναι μεγαλοψύχους . . . τοὺς δὲ ἐκ μέσης τῆς Ἑλλάδος . . . Lucian iud. voc. 7 (Sigma compains against Tau) κατηγόμην δὲ παρὰ κωμῳδιῶν τινι ποιητῇ, Λυσίμαχος ἐκαλεῖτο, Βοιώτιος μέν, ὡς ἐφαίνετο, τὸ γένος ἀνέκαθεν, ἀπὸ μέσης δὲ ἀξιῶν λέγεσθαι τῆς Ἀττικῆς· παρὰ τούτῳ δὴ τῷ ξένῳ . . . Macho in Ath. 578 B αἰσχρὸν γὰρ ὄνομα Φρυγιακὸν γυναῖκ᾿ ἔχειν, | καὶ ταῦθ᾿ ἑταίραν ἐκ μέσης τῆς Ἑλλάδος, | μὴ τὴν Ἀθηναίων γε κωλῦσαι πόλιν, | ὑφ᾿ ἧς ἅπαντές εἰσ᾿ ἐπηνορθωμένοι. Philostratus vit. soph. 2. 1. 14 τὴν δὲ δὴ γλῶτταν, ἔφη ὁ Ἡρώδης, πῶς ἐπαιδεύθης καὶ ὑπὸ τίνων; οὐ γάρ μοι τῶν ἀπαιδεύτων φαίνῃ· καὶ ὁ Ἀγαθίων, ἡ μεσογεία, ἔφη, τῆς Ἀττικῆς ἀγαθὸν διδασκαλεῖον ἀνδρὶ βουλομένῳ διαλέγεσθαι· οἱ μὲν γὰρ ἐν τῷ ἄστει Ἀθηναῖοι, μισθοῦ δεχόμενοι Θρᾴκια καὶ Ποντικὰ μειράκια καὶ ἐξ ἄλλων ἐθνῶν βαρβάρων ξυνερρυηκότα, παραφθείρονται παρ᾿ αὐτῶν τὴν φωνὴν μᾶλλον ἢ ξυμβάλλονταί τι αὐτοῖς ἐς εὐγλωττίαν· ἡ μεσογεία δὲ ἄμικτος βαρβάροις οὖσα, ὑγιαίνει αὐτοῖς ἡ φωνὴ καὶ ἡ γλῶττα τὴν ἄκραν Ἀτθίδα ἀποψάλλει. — For ὡς ἂν see on fr. 816.

lg.l: τηροῦντα τοὺς λέγοντας καὶ συνάγοντα τὰς ὀφρῦς καὶ

div.p: 1121 Eustath. Od. p. 1538, 13 τοξοποιεῖ γοῦν τὰς ὀφρῦς καὶ δεσμεῖ καὶ συνάγει ὁ σκυθρωπάζων. λέγει δέ που καὶ Σοφοκλῆς τὸ ῾τηροῦντα . . . ἐπεγείροντα,᾿ εἰπὼν τοῦτο ἐκεῖνος ὡς ἀπὸ ἰχθύων, οἱ τὰς ἀκάνθας ὀρθοῦσι καιρῷ θυμοῦ.

Brunck suspected Eustathius of a lapse of memory, and suggested Aristophanes as possibly the author of the words quoted. Subsequent editors agree with him, and no other conclusion seems possible. But the slip was probably made by his authority rather than by Eustathius himself. — There are many synonyms for σκυθρωπάζειν, such as ἀνάγειν, αἴρειν, ἀνασπᾶν τὰς ὀφρῦς. For τοξοποιεῖν, which has been compared with our to arch the eyebrows, cf. Ar. Lys. 7 μὴ σκυθρώπαζ᾿ ὦ τέκνον· | οὐ γὰρ πρέπει σοι τοξοποιεῖν τὰς ὀφρῦς (Blaydes). ὀφρῦς συνάγειν occurs in Ar. Nub. 582 (‘when you elected Cleon’) τὰς ὀφρῦς συνήγομεν, Plut. 756 ὀφρῦς ξυνῆγον ἐσκυθρώπαζόν θ᾿ ἅμα, fr. 579 (I 539 K.), and often elsewhere. Plut. def. or. 6 p. 412 F has ταῦτα συντείνει καὶ συνίστησι τὸ πρόσωπον: see on fr. 902. — The comic metaphor of τὰς ἀκάνθας ἐπεγείρειν is a tour de force, and does not occur elsewhere. — To recast the words quoted in metrical form seems hopeless.
1122 Athen. 68 A τὸ δὲ ῥῆμα (i.e. the verb: he has been quoting instances of the noun ἄρτυμα) κεῖται παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ ‘ἐγὼ...σοφῶς.’

Examples from Cratinus and Eupolis follow: amongst those of the noun which precede is fr. 675. Valckenaer conjectured that the words παρὰ Σοφοκλεῖ were a mistake for παρὰ Σωφίλῳ ἐν Ἀνδροκλεῖ, a play from which Athenaeus quotes elsewhere (123 E, 228 B); and Meineke (Com. III 584) agreed (though he thinks ἐν Ἀνδροκλεῖ unnecessary), remarking “Videntur autem illa ne satyricae quidem fabulae convenire.” Brunck too, Nauck, and Kock (III 624) are all of opinion that the words come from a comedy. The later comedy is full of cooks, and when a man sees μάγειρος ἀρτύσω in an iambic line quoted by Athenaeus, he is predisposed to suspicion that the source of it was comedy. But there are certain considerations to give us pause: (1) why should Athenaeus go so far afield as to quote Sophilus for an example of ἀρτύω? But if the word occurred with the culinary sense in Sophocles, it was another matter, parallel to the citation of ἀρτύματα, which we know to be correct; and in fact it appears that Athenaeus was seeking for the earliest occurrences of the verb. (2) The line cannot have been spoken by a cook, but must have come from some one who was comparing himself to one: render, “I'll be the cook | To dress this rarely.” If the meaning were “I, the cook,” we must have had ἐγὼ ὁ μάγειρος; and, if spoken by a man who, though not a cook, was about to act as one, the collocation ἐγὼ μάγειρος is out of place. So soon as μάγειρος is added, the cookery becomes only metaphorical. This may be illustrated by Alexis fr. 110, 18 ff. (II 335 K.), where the supposed situation actually occurs, but ἐγὼ μάγειρος is avoided: τούτοις μάγειρος οὐ πρόσεισ᾽, οὐκ ὄψεται— οἰμώξεται γὰρ νὴ Δί᾽—ἀλλ᾽ ἐγὼ σοφῶς ταῦτ᾽ οἰκονομήσω καὶ γλαφυρῶς καὶ ποικίλως | οὕτω—ποιῶ γὰρ τοὔψον αὐτός— ὥστε τοὺς | δειπνοῦντας εἰς τὰ λοπάδι᾽ ἐμβάλλειν (l. ἐκβ.) ποιῶ | ἐνίοτε τοὺς ὀδόντας ὑπὸ τῆς ἡδονῆς. This point of Greek has not been observed, e.g. by Ellendt, who, accepting the words as written by Sophocles, ascribes them to the Phaeacians, and argues that it was a satyric play.’ (H.) We have thus an example of the idiom which has been illustrated on fr. 800. See also Blaydes on Ar. Plut. 295 τράγοι δ᾽ ἀκρατιεῖσθε. Among Shorey's examples are Theogn. 347 ἐγὼ δὲ κύων ἐπέρησα χαράδρην, Cephisodor. fr. 1 ἐγὼ δὲ τοῖς λόγοις ὄνος ὕομαι. It must however be admitted, even after H.'s explanation, that the occurrence of this metaphor in a tragedy—or even in a satyr-play—would be remarkable enough; and I have left the fragment among the spuria, where it was placed by Nauck.
1123 Photius lex. p. 148, 6 κατεύχεσθαι· τὸ καταρᾶσθαι. οὕτως Πλάτων. κατεύχεσθαι τῶν Ἀχαιῶν· ἀντὶ τοῦ κατὰ τῶν Ἀχαιῶν εὔχεσθαι· οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς.

It is fairly certain that the second lemma of Photius refers to Plat. rep. 393 A ‘Do you know the beginning of the Iliad,’ ἐν οἷς ὁ ποιητής φησι τὸν μὲν Χρύσην δεῖσθαι τοῦ Ἀγαμέμνονος ἀπολῦσαι τὴν θυγάτερα, τὸν δὲ χαλεπαίνειν, τὸν δέ, ἐπειδὴ οὐκ ἐτύγχανε, κατεύχεσθαι τῶν Ἀχαιῶν πρὸς τὸν θεόν; Nauck concludes that οὕτως Πλάτων and οὕτως Σοφοκλῆς have changed places; and the allusion to Sophocles is made plain by Suid.: κατεύχεσθαι· τὸ καταρᾶσθαι. οὕτω Πλάτων. καὶ Σοφοκλῆς (O.T. 246)· κατεύχομαι δὲ τὸν δεδρακότα τάδε (δεδρακότ᾽ εἴτε τις Soph.). ἀντὶ τοῦ καταρῶμαι. καὶ Αἰλιανός κτέ. In Suidas the quotation from Plato has dropped out, just as that from Sophocles has been lost in Photius. I think, therefore, that κατεύχεσθαι τῶν Ἀχαιῶν was not a separate lemma in Photius, but represented the quotation from Plato following his name with the explanation ἀντὶ τοῦ...εὔχεσθαι, just as in Suidas the explanation ἀντὶ τοῦ καταρῶμαι follows the line from the O.T.
1124 Etym. M. p. 254, 53 δελήτιον· τὸ δέλεαρ. Σοφοκλῆς ‘ἔχε τὸ δελήτιον.’ ἢ Σώφρων (fr. 118 K.).
All critics are agreed that the words ought to be attributed to Sophron rather than to Sophocles.

1125 Etym. M. p. 207, 16 Βουθοίη (βούθοια cod. Flor. ap. Miller, p. 68) πόλις τῆς Ἰλλυρίδος. Σοφοκλῆς Ὀνομακλεῖ (σοφος ὀνο κλεῖ cod. M, σοφοκλῆς οἷον ὀνομακλεῖ cod. Flor.) ‘Βουθοίη (Βουθόη cod. Flor.) . . . ἐνάσθη.’

The corruption is obvious, and O. Schneider (Callim. II p. 637) proposed Σοφοκλῆς Οἰνομάῳ (so Gataker before him). Καλλίμαχος ‘Βουθόῃ ἥ’ κτέ. Casaubon conjectured Σοφοκλῆς ἐν Ἡρακλεῖ. Schneider was probably right in recognizing an Alexandrian fragment; but Οἰνομάῳ is unlikely, and Σοφοκλῆς may be a mere blunder. Reitzenstein, Gesch. d. Etym. p. 328, adopting a conjecture of Schwartz, restores the text (Etym. gen.) thus: Σοφοκλῆς οἷον . . . ‘οὔνομα κλειτῇ | Βουθοίῃ’ κτέ. The source was then the note of Sophocles on Ap. Rh. 4. 516. Buthoe was a town in Illyria said to have been founded by Cadmus, which received its name because he travelled from Thebes ἐπὶ βοῶν ζεύγους ταχέως (Etym. M. p. 207, 12). Euripides, though he does not mention Buthoe, was familiar with the ox-waggon : see Bacch. 1333 f. ὄχον δὲ μόσχων, χρησμὸς ὡς λέγει Διός, | ἐλᾷς μετ᾽ ἀλόχου, βαρβάρων ἡγούμενος. It is possible therefore that Sophocles referred to the legend, in the Niobe or elsewhere. Steph. Byz. p. 180, 19 (Herodian I 306, 5), gives the alternative derivation from the Egyptian Buto, which is less clearly indicated in Etym. M. The Roman name was Butua (Pauly-Wissowa III 1092).

1126 Clem. Alex. strom. 5. 14, p. 717 (Euseb. praep. ev. 13 p. 680 D, Theodoret. therap. 7 p. 109, 36) ὁ μὲν γὰρ Σοφοκλῆς, ὥς φησιν Ἑκαταῖος ὁ τὰς ἱστορίας συνταξάμενος ἐν τῷ κατ᾽ Ἄβραμον καὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους ἄντικρυς ἐπὶ τῆς σκηνῆς ἐκβοᾷ ‘εἷς ταῖς. . . νομίζομεν.’ These verses are quoted by a series of Christian writers, of whom the earliest is Justin Martyr (c. 150 A.D.) coh. ad gent. 18, de monarch. 2 p. 136. Clement of Alexandria (c. 200 A.D.) quotes them again in protrept. p. 63, and hence they passed on to Eusebius (c. 320 A.D.), to Cyril of Alexandria (contr. Iul. I p. 32 A [c. 420 A.D.]), to Theodoret (c. 450 A.D.), and to George Cedrenus (I p. 82, 9 [c. 1100 A.D.]). Vitelli (ap. Nauck) reports that they also occur in a Naples codex II F 9 fol. 140 v. Verses 1 and 2 are found in Athenag. suppl. pro Christ. 5 (c. 130 A.D.), where however they are supposed to be an interpolation.

The context is of a different character in John Malalas p. 40 ed. Bonn (c. 565 A.D.) ὁ γὰρ σοφώτατος Σοφοκλῆς δρᾶμα ἐξέθετο καὶ ποιητικῶς εἶπεν ὅτι τὴν Παλλάδα εἶδε λουομένην καὶ γυνὴ ἐγένετο. ὁ Τειρεσίας, φησί, τὴν σοφίαν τοῦ δημιουργοῦ ἐζήτησε γνῶναι καὶ οὐκ ἐδυνήθη· ὅθεν ἐξέθετο ὁ αὐτὸς Σοφοκλῆς ἐν τοῖς αὐτοῦ συγγράμμασι ταῦτα ἀληθείας εἶναι· εἷς ἔστιν ὁ θεός, ὃς τὸν οὐρανὸν ‘ἔτευξε καὶ γαῖαν μακράν . . . νομίζομεν.’ μοναρχίαν γὰρ ἐδόκει δοξάζειν ὁ αὐτὸς Σοφοκλῆς. With the first part of this extract Nauck compares Cramer, anecd. Paris. II p. 259, 4 κατὰ τούτους τοὺς χρόνους Κάδμος ὁ ἐν Θήβαις ἐβασίλευσεν, ὃς Τειρεσίαν φιλόσοφον καὶ μάντιν ἐν Θήβαις ἤγαγε, περὶ οὗ φησὶ Σοφοκλῆς ὅτι τὴν Παλλάδα ἰδὼν λουομένην ὁ Τειρεσίας μετεβλήθη ἐξ ἀνδρὸς εἰς γυναικείαν φύσιν. Cramer's publication was actually the editio princeps of the first part of the chronicle of Leo grammaticus (c. 1013 A.D.), which is said to be derived from the lost work of Sextus Iulius Africanus (c. 221 A.D.) of Alexandria, the earliest of the series of world-chronicles : see Krumbacher, p. 134. It is obvious that the two passages go back to the same original. The statement about Tiresias does not necessarily stand on the same footing as the verses quoted above. It is in fact a conflation of two stories concerning the Theban seer both of which are old, (1) that he saw Athena bathing and was in consequence blinded by her (Pherecydes fr. 50 [FHG 185] = Apollod. 3. 70, Callim. lav. Pall. 75 ff.) ; (2) that, happening to see the union of two snakes, he wounded one of them and was changed to a woman, and that subsequently, on a repetition of the same occurrence, he recovered his original sex (Apollod. 3. 71, Hesiod. fr. 162 Rz., Phlegon mir. 4). Prima facie, there would be nothing surprising in Sophocles having made use of either of these legends; but the fact of their confusion, and the suspicious character of the sources from which our information is derived, are enough to warrant a suspension of judgement.

To return to the fragment itself, it will be observed that Clement professes to rely on the authority of Hecataeus in his book relating to ‘Abraham and the Egyptians.’ Boeckh (Tr. Gr. princ. p. 148) held that this ‘Hecataeus’ was a forged document, by means of which spurious verses were attributed to the classic poets, and Susemihl (Gesch. d. gr. Lit. Alexandr. I p. 312 16) is of the same opinion. The latter points out that Hecataeus of Abdera (c. 300 B.C.) wrote a treatise Αἰγυπτιακά with romantic tendency, which contained an episode on Jewish history. This latter was undoubtedly used by Diodorus, but there is considerable difference of opinion as to whether the quotations made by Josephus from Hecataeus περὶ Ἰουδαίων were taken from the Αἰγυπτιακά, or from a Judaizer who assumed the name of Hecataeus. (Jacoby in Pauly-Wissowa VII 2765 ff.) However this may be, there is no doubt that the treatise κατ’ Ἄβραμον καὶ τοὺς Αἰγυπτίους used by Clement, which was cited also by Josephus (ant. Jud. 1. 158) as the περὶ Ἀβράμου, was the work of a forger, whose object it was to represent the Jews as the original possessors of all true wisdom, and as the instructors of other nations. For such a purpose the utility of fabricated quotations is obvious.

J. writes: ‘Bentley pointed out the general state of the facts in his Letter to Mill (ed. Dyce, vol. II p. 256 ff.), published in Mill's edition of the Chronicle of John Malalas...On the internal evidence of spuriousness Bentley makes a few remarks, one of which is just and forcible, — viz. that an Attic poet, at the Dionysia, would not have denounced Greek festivals (vv. 8, 9). But Bentley's verbal remarks are here less happy. (1) In v. 4 he gives πολλόν, and denies its use to tragedy (though Soph. has πολλόν as adv. in a trimeter, Ant. 86, and as acc. sing. masc. in Trach. 1196). A
better reading πολλοί is, however, now established. (2) In v. 6 he objects to χαλκέων, saying that it should be χαλκῶν. But Soph. has λέβητι χαλκέῳ in Trach. 556, and χρυσέων in Trach. 1099.

‘On the other hand, Bentley passes over a real mark of late date, viz. the plural ταῖς ἀληθείαισιν (= τῇ ἀληθείᾳ) in v. 1. This adverbial use occurs in Philemon fr. 130 (II 519 K.) εἰ ταῖς ἀληθείαισιν οἱ τεθνηκότες | αἴσθησιν εἶχον. In later Greek it is frequent (Polyb. 10. 40. 5 καὶ λέγεσθαι. . . καὶ ταῖς ἀληθείαις ὑπάρχειν). The earliest example is Isocr. 15. 283 (353 B.C.) καὶ ταῦτα καὶ ταῖς ἀληθείαις οὕτως ἔχει (“in respect to the realities of the case.” So Rutherford on Babr. 75. 19 ought not to say that the instance in Philemon is probably the earliest). The plural of abstract nouns was often used from the fourth century onwards: see my n. on Isocr. l.c. (Selections, p. 257).’ Bernays, who discussed the fr. in his treatise on pseudo-Phocylides p. 36, calls it ‘a capuchin's sermon against paganism. ’ There is not the slightest doubt that these verses are an impudent forgery, being probably, as we have seen, the work of an Alexandrian Jew. The late use of χαροπός (v. 3) is more remarkable than that of ταῖς ἀληθείαισιν, and the leading idea of the last six lines, — not to speak of difficulties in detail which need not be discussed here — the turning to idols of stone and trusting to them for support in time of sorrow, reads like a Hellenized paraphrase from a Hebrew prophet of the Old Testament. I should be content to rest the case on καρδίᾳ πλανώμενοι (v. 4) alone, which ought to be decisive to anyone bearing in mind Psalm 95. 10 τεσσαράκοντα ἔτη προσώχθισα τῇ γενεᾷ ἐκείνῃ, καὶ εἶπα, ἀεὶ πλανῶνται τῇ καρδίᾳ, καὶ αὐτοὶ οὐκ ἔγνωσαν τὰς ὁδούς μου. The difference is instructive; for a Greek would have said γνώμῃ, φρεσί, or διανοίᾳ πλανᾶσθαι.

It should be added that it did not seem worth while to record all the variants, for the most part unimportant, which occur in the citation of the lines by the several authorities mentioned above: those who wish for the information will find it in Nauck.

div.p: 1127. 5 νυμφικοῖς μοιχικοῖς vel μυθικοῖς Euseb. | ἐπεστάθη vel ἐπεστάτει Eus. : ἐπεσχάλη Clem.

1127 Clem. Alex. strom. 5. 14 p. 716 (recurring in Euseb. praep. ev. 13 p. 680 A) ὁ Σοφοκλῆς δὲ εὐθυρρημόνως γράφει ‘τὴν τοῦδε ... ἀνήρ’ (vv. 1-4). εἶτα ὑπελθὼν καὶ δὴ ἐπήγαγεν ‘ταχὺς... ὁ μοιχός’ (vv. 5, 6). ἐφ᾽ οἷς ἔτι φανερώτερον τὴν ἀκρασίαν τοῦ μυθοποιουμένου Διὸς ὧδέ πως ἐκδιηγεῖται ‘ὃ δ᾽... ἐθρύπτετο’ (vv. 7-9). Nauck thinks that v. 4 is referred to by Hesych. III p. 199 ὁλοσχερής...τέλειος, ὁλόκληρος : but that is very doubtful.

Porson on Eur. Med. 284 held that these lines came from a satyr-play on the following grounds: (1) ἐπημφιεσμένος violates the rule that ἀμφί like περί is not used in tragic senarii when compounded with a verb or noun beginning with a vowel: contrast Eur. Cycl. 686; (2) πτίλον, ὑπημβρύωσεν, ὁλοσχερής, and ἐθόρνυτο are not admissible in tragedy. L. Dindorf, in Steph. Thes. s.v. βαθμός p. 21 c, expresses surprise that he should have thought them admissible even in a satyr-play, and pronounces the fragment to be spurious,
adding that we ought to be on our guard against all citations which rest solely upon the authority of the Fathers.

app.rdg: Eus., cf. Hesych. II p. 22 ἐθόρνυτο·

div.p: Jebb, on the other hand, regarded it as genuine. Mentioning the words condemned by Porson, he remarks: ‘Now ἠμφιεσμένος is used by Hipponax fr. 3, Ar. Eccl. 879, Lysias and Plato: it might surely then occur in tragedy. But as to the other words, the objection seems sound. Indeed the whole tenor of the verses suits a satyr-play.’ Thus, he tacitly denies the truth of what Porson is arguing about the unelided ἀμφί : its validity as a universal rule he had contested in the Appendix on O. T. 1505.

Headlam appears to have been in agreement with Dindorf: he calls attention to the use of ὁλοσχερής, which is used in verse for the first time by Theocr. 25. 210. The adv. is a discredited variant in Isocr. 5. 135, but is cited from Diphilus (fr. 27, II 548 K.) by Antiatt. (Bekk. anecd.) p. 110, 18. The adjective appears first in Hippocrates, and then in Dioscorides, but is chiefly known from its use by Polybius. ὑπεμβρυόω occurs only here, and ἐμβρυόω not at all: it is the sort of word, H. remarks, which one would expect to find in Theophrastus. The most noticeable feature of the lines is what he calls the ‘virulence of the style’; they seem to breathe the spirit of a hostile fanaticism, intent only on exposing the moral corruption of Paganism. Now that we are able to contrast them with the description of a similar incident in the satyric Ichneutae (fr. 314, 261 ff.), the difference in tone is startling enough. On the other hand, there is nothing in the language which is demonstrably unclassical, nor would it be possible to refute anyone who should maintain that the context in Sophocles may have been of such a character as to justify the remarkable bitterness of the language. It should be added that, though the immediate context of the quotation is not suspicious, it is found in the same collection with others which are undoubted forgeries.

It is suggested that τοῦδε in v. 1 is Heracles, and that the language of vv. 4 and 7 is suitable to the visit of Zeus in the guise of the newly-arrived Amphitryon, while v. 8 recalls τὴν μίαν τριπλασιάσας νύκτα of Apollod. 2. 61 and the other authorities. For the Amphitryon of Sophocles see I p. 76. Brunck and Hartung, who also thought that the subject was the procreation of Heracles, referred the fragment to the satyric Heracles at Taenarum.
2 χρυσόμορφος, referring to the story of Danae: cf. Lycophr. 838, where Perseus is called τὸν χρυσόπατρον μόρφνον.

3 πτίλον is rare even in comedy: Starkie on Ar. Ach. 585. — κόρην Πλευρωνίαν, ‘Leda, daughter of Thestius, king of Aetolia. According to Pherecydes (FHG I 78) Leda's mother was a daughter of Pleuron: schol. on Apoll. Rhod. i 146 (Αἰτωλὶς Λήδη), who says also Ἴβυκος (fr. 41) Πλευρωνίαν αὐτὴν καλεῖ (cf. Roscher II 1922).’ (J.)
5 βαθμοῖς νυμφικοῖς, ‘the steps leading to the chamber of the νύμφη. — ἐπεστάθη = ἐπέστη (as oft. in poetry).’ (J.)
8 ὠδαγμένος, ‘stung’ with desire : from ὀδάξω. (Cf. Jebb on Trach. 770 ἀδαγμός.) For the metaphor see on fr. 841.

9 ἐθόρνυτο ‘= ἔθρῳσκε, in sexual sense. Her. 3. 109 ἐπεὰν θορνύωνται (when they procreate). Nicander Ther. 130 θορνυμένου ἔχιος (in same sense). As Porson says (Med. 284), the v.l. ἐθρύπτετο in Clement was doubtless a gloss.’ (J.)

div.p: 1128. 1 ἔσται καινὸς Clem. 5 ἐπὴν scripsi: ἐπὰν Clem. Eus., ὅταν Iust. | γὰρ ἐκτείνῃ scripsi: δ' ἐκλίπῃ vel δ' ἐκλείπῃ Iust. et Eus. codd., δ' ἐκλείπῃ Clem., ἄρ᾽ metri causa add. Grotius

1128 Justin Martyr de monarch. 3 p. 136 καὶ περὶ τοῦδε ὅτι μόνος δυνατός ἐστι καὶ τῶν ἐν τῷ βίῳ συντελουμένων πράξεων καὶ τῆς περὶ τὸ θεῖον ἀγνωσίας κρίσιν ἐνστήσασθαι, οἰκείους μάρτυρας παραστῆσαι ἔχω, καὶ πρῶτόν γε Σοφοκλέα καὶ περὶ τούτου λέγοντα ‘ἔσται γὰρ... ἀπώλεσεν.’ Clem. Alex. strom. 5. 14 p. 722 (Euseb. praep. ev. 13 p. 684 B) συνᾴδει δὲ τούτοις καὶ ἡ τραγῳδία διὰ τῶνδε ‘ἔσται γὰρ...μανεῖσα.’ καὶ μετ' ὀλίγα αὖθις ἐπιφέρει ‘ἐπὰν...ἀπώλεσε.’

These verses describe the Stoic ἐκπύρωσις, and therefore cannot have been written by Sophocles. They are, however, of no little intrinsic interest, and must have been composed by a Stoic, or at least by some one who was accurately informed respecting the tenets of that system. A knowledge of Stoic principles was widely spread from the third century B.C. onwards; the purpose of the lines appears to be didactic rather than controversial; and the language bears no marks of a late origin. If we proceed to enquire for an author likely to have versified Stoic doctrine, it is natural to think of Cleanthes ; and so far as contents and style are concerned there is no reason why he should not have written them. Indeed, the opening phrases are directly suggestive of his teaching, as will be shown below. But it is necessary to bear in mind that the extract comes from a suspicious source. Together with many genuine quotations Clement has included a number of unmistakable forgeries (Aesch. fr. 464; Eur. fr. 1030, 1031; Menand. fr. 1130; Philem. fr. 246; Diphil. fr. 138), which are also to be found in the de monarchia attributed to Justin Martyr. These are not to be assigned to the Christian apologists themselves, but were derived by them from such writings as those of pseudo-Hecataeus (fr. 1126 n., Susemihl II pp. 63256, 645); and, inasmuch as Clement twice quotes from Cleanthes (I 557, 560 Arn., frs. 75, 101 P.) in the same chapter, we should have expected to find his name attached also to the present passage, if it was actually composed by him.

‘The primitive substance (Pneuma) was determined by Chrysippus, following Zeno, to be fiery breath or αἰθήρ, a spiritualized sublimed element. This primitive substance is also the creative force, or deity, which shapes the cosmos, or universal order. Out of it the elements which we know are separated off; first, fire (as we know it); then, air or vapour (condensed fire); then water and earth, which are solidified air. But, after these elements have been separated, there remains a residue of the Pneuma or primitive substance. This residue is the αἰθήρ, in the highest sphere of the visible heavens, encircling the world, of which it is lord and head.

‘The cosmos does not remain in one state eternally, but passes through cycles of decay, destruction, and renewal. The individual things in the cosmos will be gradually resolved back into the elements, and the elements into the primary substance or Pneuma, the αἰθήρ. The end of this process will be a general conflagration, when once more the world will be absorbed into the deity (Pneuma, αἰθήρ). "Then in due order a new cycle of development begins, reproducing the last in the minutest detail, and so on for ever." (R. D. Hicks in Encycl. Brit. XII at p. 564).’ (J.) For the Stoic texts bearing on the ἐκπύρωσις see von Arnim Stoic. vet. fragm. II p. 183 ff., and for the important fragment of Cleanthes ibid. I 497 p. 111 ( = fr. 24 P.).

7 γῆ δ᾽ ἑδράνων (γῆ δὲ ἀνδρῶν F) Iust. : γῆ δὲ ἐδραν ὧν (sic) Clem., γῆ δὲ ἐράνων Eus., γῆ δενδρέων Grotius, γῆ δ᾽ ἀνέρων Conington | οὐδ᾽ ἀὴρ ἔτι Grotius : οὐδ᾽ ἄρ᾽ ἔτι Iust., οὐδὲ ἄρ᾽ ἔτι Eus., οὐ γὰρ ἐπὶ Clem. 8 βαστάσει Iust.: βλαστάσει Clem., βλαστήσει Eus. | πυρούμενος Grotius. Post hunc v. ponit Iust. καὶ γὰρ καθ' Ἅιδην δύο τρίβους νομίζομεν, | μίαν δικαίων χἁτέραν ἀδίκων ὁδόν, quae Diphilo alibi vel Philemoni (fr. 245, II 539 K.) tribuuntur

J. renders thus: ‘The day shall come, in the course of ages, when the golden ether shall release its teeming store of fire, and the flame, long fed within, shall kindle in its fury all things on the earth and in the sky. And when that conflagration has wholly ceased (ἐπὰν δ' ἄρ᾽ ἐκλίπῃ τὸ πᾶν: or “when the universe has ceased”), the sea with all its depths will have vanished, and the earth will be void of habitations [see, however, below]; and the air, full of fire, will no longer carry the winged tribes. And then the deity will restore all that he has destroyed.’

1 ff. ἔσται...ὅταν. This construction with a characterizing subordinate clause, as distinguished from a clause of general assumption, is not provided for by the ordinary grammars : see W. G. Hale, Anticipatory Subjunctive (Chicago Studies in Classical Philology I [1895], p. 19. It is obviously modelled on the pattern of Hom. Z 448 ἔσσεται ἦμαρ, ὅτ' ἄν ποτ' ὀλώλῃ Ἴλιος ἱρή. I have briefly called attention to certain Attic anomalies of this kind in C. R. XVII 249, but the subject is one which deserves fuller treatment. For the present I will only point out that Aesch. Ag. 1317 is not essentially distinct from Hom. X 358, although grammarians analyse them differently. The example in the text may be profitably compared with Isocr. 4. 138 ἢ που σφόδρα χρὴ δεδιέναι τὸν καιρὸν ἐκεῖνον, ὅταν τὰ μὲν τῶν βαρβάρων καταστῇ... ἡμεῖς δὲ πρὸς ἀλλήλους ὥσπερ νῦν πολεμικῶς ἔχωμεν. — πυρός κτέ. For the predominance of αἰθήρ at the ἐκπύρωσις cf. Dio Chrys. 40. 37 (II p. 177 R.) ἡ λεγομένη παρὰ τοῖς σοφοῖς ἐπικράτησις αἰθέρος. Ar. Did. fr. 36 (Diels, Doxogr. p. 468) ἐξαιθεροῦσθαι πάντα κατὰ περιόδους τινὰς τὰς μεγίστας εἰς πῦρ αἰθερῶδες ἀναλυομένων πάντων. Plut. comm. not. 36 p. 1077 D ὅταν οὖν ἐκπύρωσις γένηται, μόνον ἄφθαρτον ὄντα τὸν Δία τῶν θεῶν ἀναχωρεῖν ἐπὶ τὴν πρόνοιαν, εἶθ' ὁμοῦ γενομένους ἐπὶ μιᾶς τῆς τοῦ αἰθέρος οὐσίας διατελεῖν ἀμφοτέρους. The language of the present passage points to the ἐκπύρωσις of Cleanthes and his successors in the following particulars: (1) ‘The store of fire accumulated in the αἰθήρ must come from the heavenly bodies. The sun is pure fire, the stars of fiery nature. The heavenly sphere itself, or fiery zone surrounding the world, is called αἰθήρ: totum hoc caelum quod igneus aether, mundi summa pars, claudit, Senec. nat. quaest. 6. 16. 2. Now Cleanthes supposed that the conflagration originated by the sun absorbing the moon and stars: Plut. comm. not. 31 p. 1075 D (I 510 Arn., fr. 25 P.). φλόξ, it may be noticed, was the term employed by Cleanthes for the fire in which all things are consumed: Philo incorr. mund. 18 p. 254, 7 Bern. (I 511 Arn., fr. 23 P.) μεταβάλλειν δὲ ἢ εἰς φλόγα ἢ εἰς αὐγὴν ἀναγκαῖον· εἰς μὲν φλόγα, ὡς ᾤετο Κλεάνθης, εἰς δ' αὐγήν, ὡς ὁ Χρύσιππος. Conformably with this we find ἐκφλογισθέντος τοῦ πάντος in another extract from Cleanthes: Stob. ecl. I 17. 3 p. 153, 7 (I 497 Arn., fr. 24 P.). But in verse no stress can be laid on a word which it would be most natural to use, even without any reference to Cleanthes.’ R. D. Hicks (communicated to J.). (2) The description is consistent with the τόνος doctrine which, though not exclusively Cleanthean, is believed to have been first formulated by him. When the world is moving towards ἐκπύρωσις, there is a constant progress from the apparent ἰσονομία — the equilibrium of the warring forces — to the ἐπικράτησις θεοῦ (Philo de anim. sacrif. idon. 6 II p. 242 M.). This is due to the increase of tension caused by the ever-waxing force of the fiery element collected in the periphery (ἄνω φησὶν αὔξεσθαι).
At length the sun and stars discharge their teeming store throughout the cosmos, and the equilibrium is upset by a vast expansion of the compressed matter of which the world as we know it was compact. I have partly discussed this subject in Fragments of Zeno and Cleanthes, p. 252 f.: but the details cannot be made good here. See also E. V. Arnold, Roman Stoicism, p. 196. — For σχάσῃ see n. on Eur. Phoen. 454.

5 ἐπήν : see cr. n. That ἐπήν rather than ἐπάν was employed by the older Attic writers seems to be established by the MS evidence applying to Ar. Av. 1355, Lys. 1175 (neither of which passages is paratragoedic), Isocr. 5. 38. In Thuc. ἐπήν occurs three times in treaties. Modern editors follow Hermann in restoring ἐπήν against the tradition in Eur. Her. 1364. On the other hand Alexis fr. 16 (III 303 K.), as recorded, has ἐπάν. ‘ἤν and ἐπήν are foreign to all Attic inscriptions. ἐπάν occurs first in the third century (265 B.C.).’ Weir Smyth, Ionic Dial., p. 609 (cf. p. 71). Meisterhans, p. 252, agrees that ἐπήν was Ionic. It is clear that the tendency of the tradition is for ἐπήν to give way to the later ἐπάν, and here as in Eur. it is reasonable to prefer ἐπήν. — γὰρ ἐκτείνῃ: see cr. n. γάρ is occasionally ousted by δέ in our MSS (e.g. Xen. Symp. 4. 19), but the converse is far more common (fr. 873 n.). It will be seen that J. gives alternative renderings of the vulgate; but it appears that he preferred to make φλόξ the subject, as he remarks that on the other view the following clauses become somewhat tame. I think there is a much stronger reason against taking τὸ πᾶν as nominative, viz. that in the mouth of a Stoic τὸ πᾶν included the κενὸν ἄπειρον (Aët. plac. 2. 1. 7, Sext. math. 9. 332, Plut. comm. not. 30 p. 1073 E), and the phrase τὸ πᾶν ἐκλείψει would be absurd. It is true that τὸ πᾶν is often used loosely; but, because e.g. τὸ πᾶν ἐκφλογισθήσεται is intelligible, it does not follow that τὸ πᾶν ἐκλείψει could be used. The other view, that τὸ πᾶν is adverbial, is of course possible (El. 1009); but in that case it is surely very odd to read that, when the conflagration has entirely ceased, the air is still aflame (v. 8). Another equally vital objection to the text is that the cessation (or quenching) of the fiery process does not complete the destruction of the phenomenal world which is described in the following lines (that is rather the effect of the ἐπικράτησις αἰθέρος), but is the first stage in the παλιγγενεσία, which begins with the creation of the σῶμα of the new world by the operation of συστολή. This comes out most clearly in Philo incorr. mund. 19 (II 619 Arn.), which is confirmed by the various statements of Plut. Sto. rep. 41 p. 1053 B, C, Athanas. c. Arian. IV 13 p. 626, and Dio Chrys. 36. 56. These considerations condemn the otherwise attractive proposal of Heyse to alter πᾶν to πῦρ. Hence I cannot accept the ordinary text, which itself rests partly on conjecture, and propose to substitute ἐπὴν γὰρ ἐκτείνῃ, which yields a meaning consonant with Stoic principles. The phrase πῦρ ἐκτείνει τὸ πᾶν is an intelligible if illogical equivalent of πῦρ ἐκτείνεται διὰ τοῦ παντός. There was an infinite void outside the κόσμος, into which at the ἐκπύρωσις the disintegrated elements, indefinitely rarefied and extended, found room to spread. Cf. Aët. plac. 2. 4. 14 μήτε αὔξεσθαι μήτε μειοῦσθαι τὸν κόσμον, τοῖς δὲ μέρεσιν ὁτὲ μὲν παρεκτείνεσθαι πρὸς πλέονα τόπον, ὁτὲ δὲ συστέλλεσθαι. Dio Chrys. 36. 53 (of the horse of Zeus, signifying αἰθήρ), τόπον τε ὡς πλεῖστον καταλαβεῖν καὶ μείζονος χώρας δεηθῆναι τότε. Plut. comm. not. 35 p. 1077 B μετὰ τὴν ἐκπύρωσιν εἰς σπέρμα μετέβαλε τὸν κόσμον ἐκ βραχυτέρου σώματος καὶ ὄγκου χύσιν ἔχοντα πολλήν, καὶ τοῦ κενοῦ προσεπιλαμβάνοντα χώραν ἄπλετον ἐπινεμομένην τῇ αὐξήσει. Philo incorr. mund. 19 p. 507 M. (258 Bern.) ἅπαν σῶμα ἀναλυόμενον εἰς πῦρ διαλύεταί τε καὶ χεῖται, σβεννυμένης δὲ τῆς ἐν αὐτῷ φλογὸς στέλλεται καὶ συνάγεται...καὶ μὴν ὁ κόσμος ὁ πυρωθεὶς γενήσεται μείζων, ἅτε συμπάσης τῆς οὐσίας εἰς τὸν λεπτότατον ἀναλυθείσης αἰθέρα κτέ. Cleomed. circ. doctr. 1. 1 εἰ δὲ καὶ εἰς πῦρ ἀναλύεται ἡ πᾶσα οὐσία...ἀνάγκη πλέον ἢ μυριοπλασίονα τόπον αὐτὴν καταλαμβάνειν.

7 γῆ δ᾽ ἑδράνων ἔρημος. These words have been most unwarrantably suspected: see cr. n. On the other hand J.'s rendering is unsatisfactory: if the only effect of the ἐκπύρωσις upon the earth is to burn down the houses, the ἐπικράτησις θεοῦ is strangely limited in its range. Surely the meaning is rather, ‘earth is reft of its supports’; the solid earth awaits its dissolution. The best description of the whole process is in Philo incorr. mund. 19, part of which has been quoted above. The capacity of extension in the compressed earth is referred to by Cleomed. circ. doctr. 1. 11 τῷ μὲν γὰρ ὄγκῳ βραχεῖά
ἐστιν ἡ γῆ, τῇ δὲ δυνάμει μεγίστη, σχεδὸν αὐτὴ τὸ πλεῖστον τῆς οὐσίας ὑπάρχουσα. εἰ γοῦν ἐπινοήσαιμεν αὐτὴν ἢ εἰς κάπνον ἢ εἰς ἀέρα πᾶσαν ἀναλυομένην, κατὰ πολὺ ἂν μείζων γένοιτο τῆς τοῦ κόσμου περιοχῆς. The significance of ἑδράνων is to be gathered from the fact that to the Stoics the earth alone of the elements was fixed and motionless in the centre of the cosmos: Achill. isag. 4 τὴν τῆς γῆς (σφαῖραν) μόνην ἑστάναι...καὶ τὴν γῆν δέ, πανταχόθεν ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀέρος ὠθουμένην ἰσορρόπως, ἐν τῷ μέσῳ εἶναι καὶ ἑστάναι. Cf. schol. Ar. Nub. 264 καὶ οὗτος δὲ φιλοσόφων λόγος ὅτι οὐκ ἐφέδρασται (? ἐφηδρ) ἡ γῆ, ἀλλ᾽ ὑπὸ τοῦ ἀέρος πάντοθεν περιέχεται, τὸν μέσον τοῦ παντὸς λαχοῦσα τόπον. Heraclit. alleg. Hom. 41 ἑδραιότατον ἀπεφήνατο στοιχεῖον εἶναι τὴν γῆν ὥσπερ ἑστίαν τινὰ τῆς τῶν ὅλων δημιουργίας. Hence they allegorized Ἑστία as γῆ, deriving her name from ἑστάναι: Cornut. 28, Plut. qu. conv. 7. 4. 6 p. 704 B, prim. frig. 21 p. 954 F διαμένει τὸ γεῶδες· ὅθεν οὐ κατὰ χώραν μόνον ἐξ ἕδρας ἀκίνητον οὖσαν αὐτὴν ἀλλὰ καὶ κατ᾿ οὐσίαν ἀμετάβλητον Ἑστίαν κτέ. Cleanthes accused Aristarchus the Samian as κινοῦντα τοῦ κόσμου τὴν ἑστίαν, because he said that the earth moved round the sun (I 500 Arn., fr. 27 P.). The stability of the earth is common property: Hes. Theog. 117 πάντων ἕδος ἀσφαλὲς ἀεὶ | ἀθανάτων, Orph. h. 26. 4 ἕδρανον ἀθανάτου κόσμου.
9 σώσει. ‘The subject is αἰθήρ, which, in the Stoic doctrine, is itself the creative deity.’ (J.)

lg.l: νόσφι Διός· κεῖνος γὰρ ἔχει τέλος ἠδὲ καὶ ἀρχήν

div.p: 1129 Clem. Alex. strom. 5. 14 p. 726 (Euseb. praep. ev. 13 p. 688 A) Σοφοκλῆς δὲ ὁ τραγῳδοποιός ‘οὐδέ θεοῖσι’ λέγει ‘αὐθαίρετα...ἀρχήν.’

Bergk (PLG II 245 ff.) conjectures that these lines may have been taken from a paean of Sophocles. The old Ionic paean is said to have been written in hexameters, of which a trace remains in the chorus O.T. 151 ff., but those which have survived to us from a later date are in aeolic, prosodiac, or ionic metre. The chorus beginning at Trach. 205 is called by some authorities a paean to Apollo and Artemis. There is satisfactory evidence that Sophocles wrote a paean to Asclepius: see Philostr. vit. Apollon. 3. 17, Philostr. iun. imag. 14, Lucian, encom. Dem. 27. The younger Philostratus (imag. 14) quotes from it the epithet κλυτομήτης as applied to Asclepius.

H. writes : ‘Whether these verses were actually written by Sophocles it is natural to question, but when Nauck pronounces that recenti falsario debentur versus inanes et absurdi, that they certainly are not. Bergk says (II p. 248) nihil inest quod antiquo poeta sit indignum, and to my ear they have all the tone of ancient hymn or epic.’

The sentiment agrees with what is found elsewhere. The gods are subject to the ordinances of fate: Eur. I.T. 1486 τὸ γὰρ χρεὼν σοῦ τε καὶ θεῶν κρατεῖ. Simonid. fr. 5, 16 ἀνάγκᾳ δ᾽ οὐδὲ θεοὶ μάχονται. Zeus alone is absolutely free and uncontrolled: Aesch. Prom. 50 ἐλεύθερος γὰρ οὔτις ἐστὶ πλὴν Διός. Suppl. 603 ὑπ' ἀρχᾶς δ᾽ οὔτινος θοάζων | τὸ μεῖον κρεισσόνων κρατύνει; | οὔτινος ἄνωθεν ἡμένου σέβει κάτω. His supreme excellence is shown by the exact correspondence of his will with the decrees of destiny: Pind. Nem. 4. 61 τὸ μόρσιμον Διόθεν πεπρωμένον. Thus there is no movement or action which he does not guide throughout from first to last: Theocr. 17. 1 ἐκ Διὸς ἀρχώμεσθα καὶ ἐς Διὰ λήγετε, Μοῖσαι. Orph. h. ap. Stob. ecl. 1. 1. 23 p. 29, 10 Ζεὺς πρῶτος γένετο, Ζεὺς ὕστατος ἀργικέραυνος, | Ζεὺς κεφαλή, Ζεὺς μέσσα, Διὸς δ᾽ ἐκ πάντα τέτυκται.
